title: How 11 minutes a year deleted 10 days in 1582
description:
A year is about 365.2422 days. The old calendar added a leap day every 4 years, 365.25 days, which is 11 minutes too long, so it slid a full day every 128 years. By 1582 the spring equinox fell on 10 or 11 March instead of 21 March, so Pope Gregory XIII deleted 10 days: Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October. To stop the drift, century years are leap years only if they divide by 400 (1700, 1800, 1900 skipped; 2000 kept): 97 leap days every 400 years, 365.2425 days, about 27 seconds too long.

Numbers checked in code (drift rates, the 10 days, the leap rule over 100,000 random 400-year windows). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar

beats.say: Your calendar ran 11 minutes long. It cost 10 days.
Not a war, and not a plague. Just one leap day too many.
A year is 365 days and almost 6 hours. Skip them, and you're a day off every 4 years.
So add a leap day every 4 years. That's 365 and a quarter, the old Julian calendar.
But a quarter day is too much. The real year is 11 minutes shorter.
11 minutes a year is a day every 128 years. By 1582, spring arrived on 11 March, not 21 March.
So Pope Gregory deleted 10 days. Thursday the 4th of October was followed by Friday the 15th.
Then drop 3 leap days every 400 years. 1700, 1800 and 1900 skipped. 2000 stays.
Now your year runs long by 27 seconds. One day every 3,200 years.
